key_insight: HQNS makes dense QUBO optimization NISQ-friendly by solving only a small rotating frontier of variables at each stage instead of encoding the full problem at once.
engineering_relevance: This offers a practical path to run large combinatorial optimization workloads on near-term quantum hardware while controlling circuit width, two-qubit gate count, and resource usage.
method: Select a compact frontier of F << N active variables and freeze the remaining variables into reduced QUBO coefficients.
Solve each frontier with a local quantum subproblem, then rotate the frontier through a multi-stage crawling procedure to refine the global solution.
Use warm-starts, CVaR filtering, and stochastic frontier rotation to stabilize performance across stages.
evidence_signal: On MDSSP benchmarks up to N=1000, HQNS preserved 99.9908% of the mean diversity score of an 11-restart parallel SA baseline while cutting wall-clock time by 65.03%, peak CPU by 55.97%, and peak memory by 35.21%.
watch_item: Performance depends on frontier size and heuristic choices, so results may degrade if the frontier is too small or if warm-start/CVaR settings are poorly tuned.
paper_title: Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection: NISQ-Compatible Combinatorial Optimization via Stochastic Frontier Decomposition
